title: Rationalise 5 ./bin/{{prj}} scripts into a reusable framework
objective:
Build `devbin`: a single installable, declaratively configured dev-launcher framework that replaces the four hand-maintained `bin/<prj>` dispatchers in Lamplight, Baize, Conflab and Laksa with one vendored runtime plus a per-project `bin/.devbin/config.yaml`.

Done means: devbin is installed in all four projects, every command each project had before still works, the four `bin/<prj>_helpers` files and the four `bin/<prj>_help` files are gone, and a new project gets the whole surface from `devbin install` plus a config file.
context:
The four projects each carry a `bin/<prj>` dispatcher and 15-35 sibling handler scripts. Measured on 2026-08-05:

- **The dispatchers are already identical.** All four are the same 53-58 line script modulo the display name and the `<PRJ>_ROOT` variable. Conflab is the state of the art; the others have drifted.
- **32 distinct commands** across the four. Ten are universal (`build` `check` `cli` `db` `docs` `fmt` `iex` `server` `test` `version`), one is near-universal (`repl`), five appear in two projects, and sixteen are singletons. The universal set is what becomes built-in; the singletons are what the framework must let a project drop into `bin/` and have picked up automatically.
- **The helpers libraries are 50-80% the same code.** Twenty functions appear verbatim in all four files (2279 lines total). Drift has already started: `print_run_verdict` / `print_failed_log_line` and `not_yet` / `not_implemented` are the same concerns under different names in different projects.
- **The help scripts are ~92 KB of hand-maintained prose** across four copies, with no sharing, that must be edited in lockstep with the command registry.

The asset worth protecting is the **sealed-gate subsystem** -- roughly 390 lines implementing "the verdict is a file, not terminal output". It carries hard-won design rationale in-line and has propagated least evenly across the four. The fold must preserve it intact rather than reimplement it.

Full corpus analysis, the declarative/imperative boundary, and the layer architecture are in `design.md`.

wps.title: Corpus analysis and framework specification
wps.objective: Finish the corpus inventory to the depth the built-in library needs, and ratify the framework spec. The survey in `design.md` establishes the shape (32 commands, 20 shared helper functions, two-level dispatch, the sealed-gate subsystem); this WP reads the remaining behaviour so WP-08 can be specified rather than guessed.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- Per-command behavioural inventory for the 11 universal + 5 shared commands: what each does in each project, what varies, and what the variance is driven by. Recorded as a table in `design.md`.
- Complete sub-surface map for `check`, `test`, `db`, `docs`, `version`, `build` -- every subcommand in every project.
- Extraction-grammar inventory: the per-tool output grammars in `<prj>_test_{mix,credo,rust,swift,lua,shell}`, catalogued as the named library WP-06 will ship.
- The frozen `config.yaml` schema (keys, types, defaults, required-vs-optional), written as a commented reference config.
- Ratified answers to the open decisions: config format (D7), install layout, handler discovery paths, whether `bin/<prj>` becomes a symlink (D6).
- The declarative/imperative boundary written as a reviewable rule, with three worked examples from the corpus (one clearly declarative, one clearly imperative, one borderline).

## Dependencies

- None. This is the entry point.
- Blocks WP-03 (schema), WP-06 (grammars) and WP-08 (built-in behaviour).

wps.title: Project skeleton and BATS harness
wps.objective: Stand up the Devbin repository itself: the directory layout the framework is developed in, the BATS test harness every later WP writes tests into, and the local gates that keep it honest. Nothing here ships to a target project except by way of later WPs.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- Repository layout: `bin/` (the dispatcher under development), `lib/` (the runtime that gets vendored), `lib/cmd/` (built-ins), `tests/`.
- BATS harness per `intent/llm/ARCHITECTURE-shell.md`: `tests/unit/*.bats`, `tests/lib/test_helper.bash`, each test in its own temp dir, never touching `$HOME` or real project state. The assertion vocabulary matches Utilz's helper deliberately, so the two suites read as one family; deviations are noted inline with their reason.
- A fixture project generator: creates a throwaway project tree with a `bin/`, a `config.yaml` and stub handlers, so dispatcher and resolution tests have something to dispatch into.
- Gate script running `bash -n`, `shellcheck` and `intent critic shell` over the tree, plus the BATS suite; wired so it can back a pre-commit hook.
- `.github/workflows/tests.yml` modelled on Utilz's: Ubuntu, macOS (the only runner that can catch a bash 4+ construct against the 3.2 target), a no-`yq` job proving the pure-bash config fallback of D7, and a **blocking** shellcheck job that does not exclude test helpers.
- First entries in `intent/llm/MODULES.md` -- the registry rows for the dispatcher and the runtime library, registered before the files exist.
- Baseline commit of the Intent scaffold, a `.gitignore`, and a `.gitkeep` wherever an empty tracked directory is needed.

## Dependencies

- None; runs in parallel with WP-01.
- Blocks every WP from WP-03 onward -- they all write BATS tests into this harness.

wps.title: Config schema and reader
wps.objective: Implement the declarative surface: the `bin/.devbin/config.yaml` schema frozen in WP-01, and the reader that makes it available to the dispatcher and every handler, on bash 3.2, with and without `yq` installed.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/config` -- the reader. Accessors `cfg_load`, `cfg_load_string`, `cfg_get <path> [default]`, `cfg_has`, `cfg_list <path>`, `cfg_validate`, `cfg_dump`. **One** implementation: a single awk pass flattening the document to `path<TAB>value`, then pure-bash lookups over the cached text, so a dispatch costs one fork rather than one per key.
- The restricted YAML subset, documented and enforced: two-space indent, no tabs, no anchors or aliases, no block scalars, no flow collections, no sequences of maps, no duplicate keys, no jumped indent. Anything outside it is a loud error naming file and line, never a silent misread (`IN-AG-NO-SILENT-001`).
- Schema validation by path structure, not by glob: unknown keys and wrong nesting depth each fail with the offending path.
- `lib/config.reference.yaml` -- fully commented, every key with its default.
- BATS coverage: the accepted grammar, every promised rejection, the accessors, schema validation, and bash 3.2 execution.

## Revised during the WP

D7 originally specified **two** backends -- `yq` when present, pure-bash otherwise -- reconciled by a differential test. Dropped in favour of a single awk reader. The reasons are recorded in `design.md` under D7; in short, two implementations of one concern is the Highlander breach the differential test was paying for, the second backend is unreachable once the subset is enforced, and no dependency serves "works on a fresh checkout" better than an optional one does.

## Dependencies

- WP-01 (frozen schema), WP-02 (harness).
- Blocks WP-04, WP-07, WP-08.

## Notes

The dual-backend requirement is the risk in this WP. If the differential test proves expensive to keep green, the fallback is JSON via `jq` (the alternative recorded in `design.md`), which removes the second backend entirely at the cost of comments in the config file. Decide before WP-04 depends on it, not after.

wps.title: Dispatcher and command resolution
wps.objective: Build `bin/devbin` and the resolution rules behind it. This is the fold of the four identical dispatchers plus the discovery mechanism that makes dropping a script into `bin/.devbin/cmd/` sufficient to register a command.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `bin/devbin` -- symlink-safe self-resolution into `BIN_DIR` + project root, config load, resolve, `exec`. Target ~80 lines; a thin coordinator, no business logic (`IN-AG-THIN-COORD-001`).
- Resolution implementing D2 in order: `cmd/<name>` project handler, then the config `commands:` mapping, then the built-in library, then exit 2 with a help hint.
- Recursive sub-dispatch per D3: one resolution function applied at each level, so `devbin test mix` and `devbin check compile` route by the same rule as `devbin test`.
- `all` as a reserved sub-verb per D8: resolution synthesises it for any command with more than one declared option, a project handler may not shadow it, and bare `<cmd>` with no option prints that command's help rather than running everything.
- Auto-discovery: a glob over `cmd/`, no registry to hand-maintain. The `<PRJ>_COMMANDS` string in the corpus is what this replaces.
- Root and identity: project root derived from the dispatcher's real location; display name and short alias from config, not from `$0`, so `bin/conflab -> devbin` works (D6).
- `parse_common_opts` contract preserved -- `--env`, plus the bash 3.2 safe args-array idiom the corpus uses.
- Exit-code contract preserved: `0` ok, `1` die, `2` unknown command, `3` not built yet.
- BATS coverage: dispatch from any CWD, through one symlink and through two, project handler shadowing a built-in, config-mapped name (the `myls` file serving the `ls` command), unknown command, no-args help, `-v`, synthesised `all`, and the refusal to let a handler shadow `all`.

## Dependencies

- WP-02 (harness), WP-03 (config reader).
- Blocks WP-07, WP-08, WP-09.

wps.title: Runtime library: the universal helpers fold
wps.objective: Fold the twenty helper functions that appear in all four projects into one vendored library, resolving the drift the corpus has already accumulated. This is the Highlander WP: 2279 lines across four files become one.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/helpers` -- the universal twenty: `_set_env` `assert_semver` `die` `init_run_colors` `is_command` `note_promotion` `ok` `open_run_log` `parse_common_opts` `purge_only_run_logs` `purge_run_logs` `read_version` `refuse_purge_without_log` `require_tool` `rlwrap_exec` `step` `strip_ansi` `warn` `warn_if_tee_failed` `write_errors_file`. Sourced, never executed; defines functions and sets no shell options.
- Drift adjudication, one ruling each, recorded in `design.md` with the reason:
  - `print_run_verdict` (Conflab, Baize) vs `print_failed_log_line` (Lamplight, Laksa) -- one name, one implementation.
  - `not_yet` (Conflab, Baize) vs `not_implemented` (Laksa) -- likewise.
  - `check_*` (three projects) vs `run_*` (Laksa) function prefix.
  - `abs_path`, `in_keepset`, `latest_pointer_keepset` -- present in two of four; promote or drop.
- Project-name parameterisation: the corpus hard-codes the project name in the `die` / `warn` prefixes and in `<PRJ>_ROOT`. Replace with config-derived values without adding a config lookup to every call site.
- Load guard (`_DEVBIN_HELPERS_LOADED`) so double-sourcing is free, matching the corpus idiom.
- BATS coverage per function, including the bash 3.2 array idiom under `set -u`.

## Dependencies

- WP-02 (harness), WP-03 (config reader, for the name parameterisation).
- Pairs with WP-06 -- the run-log functions listed above are its surface; keep the split at the file boundary, not mid-subsystem.

wps.title: Sealed-gate subsystem
wps.objective:
Port the sealed-gate subsystem -- "the verdict is a file, not terminal output" -- into the framework intact, and generalise it into a runner that a declared gate can drive.

This is the highest-value code in the corpus (~390 of Conflab's 833 helper lines) and the least evenly propagated across the four projects. It is a **port, not a rewrite**: the in-line rationale references specific past incidents, and reimplementing from the description would lose exactly the edge cases that rationale exists to record.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/runlog` -- the subsystem, ported from Conflab with its comments: `open_run_log`, `write_errors_file`, `note_promotion`, `strip_ansi`, `purge_run_logs`, `purge_only_run_logs`, `refuse_purge_without_log`, `latest_pointer_keepset`, `in_keepset`, `warn_if_tee_failed`, the verdict printer.
- Invariants preserved, each covered by a test:
  - `.errors` opens with an in-flight marker and is sealed at run end, so it is empty exactly when a **completed** run was green; an aborted run reads as not-green.
  - The run log keeps its ANSI escapes; the sealed `.errors` is stripped, because that is the artifact a human quotes.
  - A promotion is appended to the log, not merely printed, so the judgement survives in the artifact.
  - `LATEST_*` symlinks are a convenience and never the verdict; each run prints its own absolute seal path.
  - A failed `ln` or a failed append warns and never sinks the run.
- Generic gate runner: given a name, a command line, a grammar and a log suffix, run it, seal it, report. This is what lets `check compile` be fully declared (D1).
- Aggregate runner backing the synthesised `all` (D8): runs every declared option in declared order, does **not** stop at the first breach, leaves each option's own seal intact, prints a summary naming the failures and pointing at their seal files, honours `in_all: false` by listing the option as skipped, and exits non-zero if any option failed. This one function replaces the eight hand-written `test_all` / `check_all` bodies in the corpus.
- Named extraction-grammar library from the WP-01 inventory: `mix`, `credo`, `cargo`, `xcodebuild`, `lua`, `shell`, `generic`. Each is data plus a small reader, kept beside the writer so writer and grammars stay one concern.
- Concurrency test: two runs in the same tree must not corrupt each other's seals or mislead through the shared `LATEST_*` pointers.

## Dependencies

- WP-01 (grammar inventory), WP-02 (harness), WP-05 (helpers).
- Blocks WP-08 -- every `check` and `test` built-in runs through this.

wps.title: Help system: generated listing, authored detail
wps.objective: Replace ~92 KB of hand-maintained help heredocs across four projects with a generated global listing plus authored per-command detail, so the command surface can never drift from the registry while the authored prose survives.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `devbin help` -- the grouped global listing, generated at run time from each command's declared summary, group and order. No hand-maintained list anywhere (D4).
- `devbin help <cmd>` -- authored long-form from `bin/.devbin/help/<cmd>.md`, falling back to the summary when no file exists. Sub-topics resolve the same way (`help test mix`).
- Self-describing handlers: a `# devbin: summary = ...` / `# devbin: group = ...` header block, so a script dropped into `cmd/` appears in help with no config edit. Config takes precedence over the header when both are present, and the precedence is stated in the reference config.
- **Project-specific commands are first-class in help.** A handler dropped into `cmd/` gets the same treatment as a built-in: authored detail at `bin/.devbin/help/<cmd>.md`, a place in the global listing under its declared group, its own sub-option list, and a synthesised `all` if it has more than one option. A project may also declare a preamble block shown above the listing -- the corpus's `NOT the product` disambiguation note is the reference case. Prose and the author-facing guide are WP-12; this WP delivers the machinery and its tests.
- Output shape matched to the corpus: grouped sections with headings, two-column alignment, the shared-options block, the `NOT the product` style of disambiguation note carried as a config-declared preamble.
- Drift test: for every registered command, help must list it; for every listed command, resolution must find it. This test is the reason the generated listing is worth building.
- **`devbin help --why`** -- the same generated listing, plus where each command resolved from (project handler, config, or built-in) and, for each command and option that is NOT offered here, the reason. `option_unavailable_reason` and `command_unavailable_reason` already compute those sentences and nothing surfaces them, so D2's resolution order and D11's language scoping are currently invisible: a project where `test mix` is inactive shows nothing at all, which reads as devbin being broken rather than as configuration.

  This was carried for a while as a separate `devbin list` command and hv ratified folding it in here instead (2026-08-05). Help already enumerates the surface, so a second command that also enumerates it is the Highlander breach; and "why is this not here?" is naturally asked of the listing that omits it.
- Migration pass over the four existing `<prj>_help` files: extract every authored topic into `help/<cmd>.md` files. Nothing authored is discarded without an explicit ruling.

## Dependencies

- WP-03 (config), WP-04 (resolution -- the drift test needs both halves).

wps.title: Built-ins: Gates (check, test)
wps.objective: Ship `check` and `test`: the two commands with the widest sub-surface and the highest value, built on WP-06's sealed-gate runner. Every gate is a config declaration -- name, command, grammar, log suffix -- with no per-project shell.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- **The catalogue.** `lib/builtins`: one table carrying language, grammar, log suffix, command line and summary for every built-in option. Moved out of `lib/resolve`, not copied.
- **Universal `check` gates**: `compile`, `format`, `deps`, `toolchain`, `critic`. **Shared**: `clippy`. `parity` is deliberately absent -- two bespoke implementations sharing only a name.
- **Universal `test` gates**: `mix`, `credo`. **Shared**: `rust`, `swift`, `lua`, `shell`.
- **`all` on a multi-option command** (D8), synthesised from the declared option list rather than written per command, so declaring an option is what puts it in `all`. Delivered here because Gates is where it first had real users; the other five families inherit it working.
- **One rig (D19)**: a config-declared option that declares `log:` seals through the same runner a built-in uses.
- BATS coverage for the gate families, and the two tier-1 gates (`toolchain`, `critic`) ported with their real logic.
- **The gate families exercised end to end against a real toolchain**, to the extent this repo can: Devbin declares only `shell`, so its own `check all` / `test all` run the shipped shell gates for real in CI on both platforms. The elixir, rust and swift gates have no toolchain here to run against and are exercised at WP-10 and WP-11, where the projects that have one are migrated. Recorded rather than dropped -- the original deliverable was written before it was settled that Devbin is a shell-only project.

## Dependencies

- WP-01 (behavioural spec), WP-03 (config), WP-04 (dispatch), WP-05 (helpers), WP-06 (gate runner).
- Blocks WP-10, **together with WP-14 through WP-18** -- Conflab needs the whole built-in surface, not just its gates.

## Notes

Gates went first because they carry the most value and prove the declarative boundary holds. That proof is what made the rest of the split safe to sequence: the machinery is uniform across all six families (a command name, an option, a `run:`, a sealed verdict, a synthesised `all`), and D19 is what makes that literally true rather than nearly true.
wps.preamble: Originally "Built-in command library", covering all six families. Its own notes said to split once WP-01 had specified the per-command behaviour; WP-01 closed and the split happened. This WP keeps the Gates family it delivered; **Surfaces, Build+Format, Data, Docs+Version and Shared-optional moved to WP-14 through WP-18** in that order. The deliverables moved rather than being copied -- a WP whose ACs are green while its deliverables sit elsewhere is an incomplete contract, not finished work.

wps.title: Install, upgrade, doctor
wps.objective: Make devbin installable into a project and upgradeable afterwards, with drift from the vendored copy detectable rather than silent.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `devbin install [--into <project>]` -- vendors `bin/devbin` and `lib/` into the target's `bin/`, scaffolds `bin/.devbin/` with a starter `config.yaml`, and offers the project-named and short-alias symlinks (D6). Idempotent; refuses to clobber an existing install without `--force`.
- `devbin upgrade` -- re-syncs the vendored files from the source of truth, reports what changed, and refuses to silently overwrite a file that differs from its recorded checksum.
- `manifest.sha256` -- checksum of every vendored file, written at install and verified at upgrade. This mirrors how Intent manages skills, so the operational model is already familiar (D5).
- `devbin doctor` -- verifies the install: dispatcher executable, config parses and validates against the schema, every declared command resolves, no orphaned handler in `cmd/`, YAML inside the restricted subset, symlinks intact, bash version noted.
- `devbin new <cmd>` -- scaffolds a project-specific command from templates: handler with its `# devbin:` header, ~~`cmd/<name>.yaml` metadata sidecar~~ (see below), `help/<name>.md` stub, and a `.bats` test stub. Modelled on Utilz's `opt/utilz/tmpl/` set, which is what turns "drop a script in and it works" from a claim into a one-command operation.
- ~~`devbin list`~~ -- **NOT BUILT. hv ratified folding it into WP-07 as `devbin help --why` on 2026-08-06** (D24); this line should have been struck then and was not. `help --why` prints exactly what the deliverable asks for -- the registered surface, built-in and project, with where each resolved from -- plus everything devbin ships that is not offered here and why. The debugging surface splits along a real seam instead: `help --why` explains resolution, `doctor` finds a broken install.
- Uninstall path documented and tested: removing `bin/devbin`, `bin/.devbin/lib/`, the manifest and the symlinks leaves a clean tree with the project's own `config.yaml`, `cmd/` and `help/` intact.
- BATS coverage: install into a fresh fixture, upgrade with and without local edits, doctor against a deliberately broken install.

**Two deliverables above are deliberately not built**, recorded as D24 in `design.md` and asserted as absences in `install.bats` rather than left to be noticed:

- `list` -- hv ratified folding it into `help --why` on 2026-08-06. **This file was not updated when that ruling was taken**, so the specification and the decision disagreed for a day and WP-09 re-derived a settled question. The lesson is D23's, applied to process rather than code: a ratified decision has to land in the document it changes, not only in the channel it was taken in.
- `new`'s `cmd/<name>.yaml` metadata sidecar -- superseded by the handler's own `# devbin:` header (D23). A sidecar would be a third source for a field that is supposed to have exactly one.

## Dependencies

- WP-03 (config, for the schema check), WP-04 (dispatch, for the resolution check).
- Blocks WP-10 -- the reference migration installs through this path rather than by hand.

wps.title: Reference migration: Conflab
wps.objective: Migrate Conflab -- the state of the art, and the project devbin was largely derived from -- onto the framework. This is the proof: if devbin cannot carry Conflab without loss, the design is wrong, and it is cheaper to find that out here than across four projects.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `devbin install` into Conflab, with `bin/conflab` and `bin/cf` as symlinks to it.
- `bin/.devbin/config.yaml` reproducing Conflab's full surface: all 18 commands, both `--env` and `--bin` common options, the eight `check` gates, the four `test` gates, the six version sidecars.
- The six Conflab-specific commands (`app` `daemon` `use` `release` `macos` `deploy`) repackaged as project handlers under `bin/.devbin/cmd/`, per the devbin protocol. These are the first real exercise of the project-specific path.
- Conflab-specific helpers (`crate_dir`, `macos_app_bundle`, `resolve_native_bin`, `report_provenance`, the git-stamp family, ...) relocated to a project-local library that devbin sources.
- Deletion of `bin/conflab_helpers` (833 lines) and `bin/conflab_help` (24 KB), with their content accounted for: folded, relocated, or explicitly dropped with a reason.
- Equivalence evidence: every command and subcommand that worked before works after, captured as a before/after transcript. The sealed gates are compared on their seal files, not their terminal output.
- The existing bare shims (`bin/server`, `bin/deploy`, `bin/repl`, ...) verified unchanged and still working.

## Dependencies

- WP-07, WP-09, WP-12, and the whole built-in surface: **WP-08 (Gates) plus WP-14 through WP-18** (Surfaces, Build+Format, Data, Docs+Version, Shared-optional). Conflab exercises all six families, so a partial built-in library cannot carry it.
- **WP-13 (the pre-rollout review gate) must have passed.** This is a hard gate: no project is touched before the owner has reviewed the base and ratified it.
- Blocks WP-11 -- no other project migrates until Conflab is green.

## Notes

Conflab is live and a broken launcher blocks all work in it. No branches (D10) -- quiesce Conflab, migrate inline, in this order:

1. Install devbin **alongside** the existing launcher. `bin/devbin` and `bin/.devbin/` do not touch the `bin/conflab_*` namespace, so both launchers work at once and nothing is at risk yet.
2. Build the config and the project handlers, verifying each command against the old launcher as it goes.
3. Complete the equivalence evidence with both launchers still present.
4. Only then take the `bin/conflab` and `bin/cf` symlinks and delete `bin/conflab_helpers` + `bin/conflab_help` -- as a **delete-only commit**, so undo is a single revert.

Step 4 is the only irreversible step and it happens once, last, with the evidence already in hand.

wps.title: Fleet migration: Laksa, Baize, Lamplight
wps.objective: Migrate the remaining three projects, in ascending order of divergence from the state of the art. Each migration is expected to surface framework gaps; those are fixed in devbin rather than worked around in the project, which is the whole point of the exercise.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

Per project, the same shape as WP-10 -- install, config, project handlers, project-local helpers, deletion of the old `_helpers` and `_help` files, equivalence evidence:

- **Laksa** (15 commands, 424-line helpers, 2 project-specific functions) -- least divergent, migrate first. Carries `content` `products` `log` `precommit` as project handlers. Its `run_*` check prefix and `not_implemented` naming are adjudicated in WP-05; apply the ruling here.
- **Baize** (15 commands, 474-line helpers, 3 project-specific functions) -- carries `cv` `perf` `which` `publish`. Its `rack_task` helpers and `test shell` gate are the first exercise of a gate grammar that no other project has.
- **Lamplight** (22 commands, 548-line helpers, umbrella layout) -- most divergent and largest surface, migrate last. Carries nine project-specific commands (`wrighter` `control` `canon` `contract` `media` `models` `desktop` `story` `publish`) plus `media_covers` / `media_shrink` sub-handlers, a `lamplight_helpers.d/` directory and a `lamplight_macos.d/` tree. Expect the umbrella root resolution to differ from a single-app project.
- Fleet-wide verification: all four projects on one devbin version, `devbin doctor` green in each, four `config.yaml` files as the only per-project difference in the launcher layer.
- Final accounting: lines of shell deleted across the fleet against lines added in Devbin.

## Dependencies

- WP-10 green.

## Notes

No branches (D10). Each project is quiesced and migrated inline using the four-step sequence proven in WP-10: install alongside, build config and handlers, prove equivalence, then take the symlinks and delete the old files in one delete-only commit.

**One project at a time.** A half-migrated fleet is the state this ST exists to remove, not a state to pass through -- finish Laksa before starting Baize.

**Lamplight's `server all` collided with the reserved `all`; hv resolved it by making the targets an ARGUMENT rather than an option set.** Found while reading the corpus for WP-14. `bin/lamplight_server` takes an umbrella target -- `storyfield`, `frontdesk` or `all` -- where `all` means "one process at the umbrella root serving both surfaces". Devbin reserves `all` for "run every declared option, in order" (D8), so declaring those targets as options would have started Storyfield, waited for it to exit, then started Frontdesk. Same word, quietly different behaviour, presenting as a hang.

The resolution (hv, 2026-08-05) is a comma-separated instance list with optional ports:

```
bin/lamplight server frontdesk[:port],storyfield[:port] --iex
```

This dissolves the collision rather than working around it. Instances are an **argument**, not an option set, so `server` is an option-less command, devbin never synthesises an `all` for it, and there is nothing left to collide. Devbin already carries the shape end to end -- the comma list passes through untouched, `--iex` is consumed and exported, and a bare `server` runs -- so **no framework change is needed for this**. The parity work is Lamplight's:

- **Parsing the instance list and booting the named endpoints** is a project handler. Devbin has no opinion about umbrella apps and should not acquire one.
- **Two instances in one BEAM already works** -- that is exactly what today's `server all` does, `cd $LAMPLIGHT_ROOT` then `mix phx.server`, both endpoints up on :4002 and :4003.
- **A SUBSET in one BEAM is the genuinely new part.** Today `server storyfield` cds into `apps/storyfield` and runs that app alone. Serving one named endpoint *from the umbrella root* means suppressing the other's endpoint at runtime rather than by directory, which is Elixir-side work, not a launcher concern.
- **`[:port]` needs each endpoint's port to come from the environment.** They are configured per app today; overriding per instance means each app's dev config reading its own variable. Doable and ordinary, but it is a change to Lamplight's Elixir config that devbin cannot grant.

**`wrighter` takes `--iex` too**, with the same conditional shape as `server`, so both are covered by D20 rather than by hand-rolled parsing. Note what the corpus actually does there: `wrighter --iex` runs `iex -S mix`, while plain `wrighter` runs `mix run -e "Wrighter.Desktop.Launcher.announce()" --no-halt`. The iex form is a **second command line, not a prefix on the first** -- see D20.

Framework changes made during this WP invalidate the projects already migrated. Re-run `devbin upgrade` plus the equivalence check across every migrated project after each framework change, rather than at the end -- three projects drifting apart mid-migration is the exact failure mode being eliminated.

wps.title: Documentation: README, help authoring, command-author guide
wps.objective: Write the documentation a person needs to install devbin into a project they own and add their own commands to it, without reading the framework source. The `help` *machinery* is WP-07; this WP is the prose that machinery serves, plus the front door.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- **`README.md`** -- Devbin's front door: what it is and what it replaced, install into a project, the 60-second config, the full command surface, the layout of `bin/.devbin/`, and the bash 3.2 / `yq`-optional constraints. Written for someone who has never seen the four source projects.
- **Config reference** -- every `config.yaml` key with type, default, and a worked example. Generated from, or diff-tested against, the commented reference config produced in WP-03, so the doc cannot drift from the schema.
- **Command-author guide** -- the protocol for adding a project-specific command end to end: drop a script into `bin/.devbin/cmd/`, the `# devbin:` header block that gives it a summary and a group, where its long-form help lives, how to give it sub-options, and how `all` picks those options up (D8). Includes the contrived-`ls` walkthrough from the original brief as the worked example.
- **Extended per-project help** -- documented and tested: a project-specific command's help must be a first-class citizen. `devbin help <projcmd>` renders authored detail from `bin/.devbin/help/<projcmd>.md`, the global listing shows it in its declared group alongside the built-ins, and a project may add a config-declared preamble block (the corpus's `NOT the product` disambiguation note is the reference case).
- **Migration guide** -- how to take an existing `bin/<prj>` launcher onto devbin, as the four-step quiesce-and-inline sequence from D10. Written from WP-10's actual experience, not ahead of it.
- **`intent/llm/ARCHITECTURE-shell.md` reconciliation** -- the project's own architecture doc currently prescribes `bin/<command>_helpers` and `lib/`; update it to describe what devbin actually became.

## Dependencies

- WP-03 (schema, for the config reference), WP-07 (help machinery), WP-09 (install, for the install instructions).
- The migration guide section trails WP-10.

## Notes

Scheduled after WP-09 and before WP-10 so the reference migration follows a documented protocol rather than inventing one that gets written up afterwards. The migration-guide section is the one part that is deliberately written last.

wps.title: Pre-rollout end-to-end review gate (Fable)
wps.objective:
A complete end-to-end review of the built framework, run with Fable, **after the base is built and before it touches any real project**. Owner-requested (2026-08-05) and owner-triggered.

This is a hard gate, not a checkpoint. WP-10 migrates Conflab -- a live project where a broken launcher blocks all work -- so the last moment a design error is cheap to fix is the moment before that migration starts. After WP-10 the framework has a consumer, and every correction has to be made compatibly.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- **Readiness signal to the owner.** cc announces when WP-01..09 and WP-12 are green and the base is reviewable. The owner turns the review on; cc does not start it.
- **The review pack** -- what the reviewer needs in one place:
  - The framework as built: dispatcher, config reader, runtime library, sealed gates, help, built-in commands, install path.
  - `design.md` decisions D1..D10 with, for each, whether the built thing actually honours it.
  - The declarative/imperative boundary (D1) tested against the built config: what a project can express, and what it cannot.
  - Test and gate evidence: `tests/gate all` output, coverage of what is and is not tested.
  - A written statement of what was NOT built, and why.
- **Findings triaged** into: fix before WP-10, fix during rollout, accept with a recorded reason.
- **Owner ratification** that the base is fit to roll out, recorded in `design.md`.

## Dependencies

- WP-01 through WP-09 green, plus WP-12 (the reviewer reads the docs as part of the review -- documentation that only makes sense to its author is a finding).
- **Blocks WP-10 absolutely.** No project is migrated before this gate passes.

## Notes

The framework has no consumers at this point, so a finding that says "the design is wrong" is still cheap. That property disappears the moment WP-10 lands. Anything that would be expensive to change later -- the config schema, the resolution order, the sealed-gate contract, the install layout -- gets the most scrutiny here.

wps.title: Built-ins: Surfaces (server, iex, cli, repl)
wps.objective: Ship the four process launchers. They are the thinnest family by volume and the most foundational by consequence: they are the first built-ins with **no option set** and the first that must **replace** the dispatcher process rather than run under it. Every later family inherits both answers.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- **The command-level rig, which is missing.** D19 wired the one rig for *options*; a command-level `run:` was never wired at all. `command_active` treats `commands.<cmd>.run` as making a command active, so it lists in help and then exits 3 "not built yet" -- and that is the exact shape `lib/config.reference.yaml` documents. Surfaces are the commands that have a `run:` and no options, which is why the gap surfaces here. `run_command` is the command-level twin of `run_option`, same resolution order, same `log:` rule.
- `iex`, `server`, `cli`, `repl` resolve and run with nothing declared in config.
- **Command-level summaries in the catalogue.** Every built-in currently shows a blank summary column in `help`, because the catalogue carries option rows only.
- **An option-less command carries its command line in the ONE catalogue.** `lib/builtins` is keyed `<command>.<option>`; a surface has no option and today has no row. Widening that key beats a second table -- AC-08.1 exists because two tables describing the same built-ins drift.
- **`cli` composes from `project.name`** rather than the catalogue gaining templating. The table is data; interpolation would walk it toward the `eval` boundary D1 holds.
- **`repl`** on WP-05's `rlwrap_exec`, with its history file resolved per project.
- **`server`'s `--iex` variant**, which depends on D20 (how a shipped handler reads a shared option whose exported name the project chose). Blocked on that decision, not on this WP.
- **Exec semantics for a launcher.** D19 runs a declared `run:` in a subshell at the project root -- correct for a gate, wrong for a REPL, where it leaves a shell between the terminal and the process.
- **A D18 correction**: the four surfaces are not uniformly tier 3. `iex` is; `cli` and `repl` carry real logic and `server` carries a conditional.
- BATS coverage per command against the fixture project.

## Dependencies

- WP-04 (dispatch), WP-05 (`rlwrap_exec`), WP-08 (the catalogue and its readers).
- D20 gates the `server --iex` deliverable only; the other three proceed without it.
- Interacts with **AC-04.13**: that AC says a bare `<cmd>` prints the command's help, which is right for a multi-option command and wrong for a surface -- `devbin server` must launch the server. Reword before this lands or the two contradict.
- Blocks WP-10.

## Notes

First of the five family packages, and first for the right reason. The board called this the cheapest of them; reading the code against D18 says otherwise. It goes first because the questions it forces -- option-less commands, shared-option visibility, exec-versus-subshell -- are cheaper to answer on four thin launchers than on `version`, whose sidecar sync has already shipped one defect in Conflab.
wps.preamble: Split out of WP-08 (built-in command library) along the family cut WP-08's own notes named. Sequenced at position 8, after the Gates family; the number is an ID, not a schedule.

wps.title: Built-ins: Build and format
wps.objective: Ship `fmt`, and prove `build` needs nothing shipped but the rig. These two are the clearest demonstration of the declarative boundary: one has defaults worth shipping and the other deliberately has none.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/cmd/fmt` implementing the catalogued options (`fmt.elixir`, `fmt.rust` exist in `lib/builtins`; `md` and `swift` per the corpus), plus the synthesised `fmt all`.
- **`build` routing with no default option set** (D18 tier 4). The command name resolves, declared targets run, `all` is synthesised in declared order, each seals. AC-08.4 already holds the negative half of this; this WP holds the positive half -- that a project's declared targets actually work end to end.
- **The `fmt` / `check format` pairing preserved.** `fmt` mutates, `check format` gates the same concern read-only. The corpus keeps them consistent by hand; devbin must keep the names and the underlying command in agreement by construction.
- BATS coverage, including a project whose `build` targets are entirely its own.

## Dependencies

- WP-08 (catalogue), WP-06 (gate runner, since `fmt` and `build` targets seal).
- Blocks WP-10.
wps.preamble: Split out of WP-08 (built-in command library) along the family cut WP-08's own notes named.

wps.title: Built-ins: Data (db)
wps.objective: Ship the small declarative core of `db` and let the variance land where it belongs. D18 found `db` has the widest project spread in the corpus: the option NAMES agree 3/4 while the commands behind them do not (`mix ash.setup` / `mix setup` / `mix ecto.setup`).
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/cmd/db` implementing the catalogued core (`setup`, `migrate`, `reset`, `seed` are already in `lib/builtins`), each overridable in one line of config.
- `codegen`, `sql` and `proxy` handled as declared options or project handlers rather than shipped defaults -- they are where the corpus disagrees most.
- **AC-04.12's recursive sub-dispatch** (`db sql <statement>`), carried here from WP-04. This is its natural home: `db sql` is the corpus's only real three-level command, so the general mechanism and its first real user land together rather than the mechanism landing speculatively.
- BATS coverage, including two projects whose `db setup` differ.

## Dependencies

- WP-04 (dispatch, and AC-04.12 which this WP discharges), WP-08 (catalogue).
- Blocks WP-10.
wps.preamble: Split out of WP-08 (built-in command library) along the family cut WP-08's own notes named.

wps.title: Built-ins: Docs and version
wps.objective: Ship `version` -- the one command D18 tiers as real shared logic across all four projects -- and `docs`. This is the family with the most genuine code in it and the one carrying the most risk, because the sidecar-sync concern has already produced a shipped defect in Conflab.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- `lib/cmd/version` with `show`, `set` and `bump` on one semver implementation, reading the file named by `project.version_from`. WP-05 already ships `read_version` and `assert_semver`; this is the command surface over them.
- **Sidecar sync, ported carefully.** In Conflab the version is the single source of truth for six files, and keeping them in step has failed once already in production. The sidecar list is per-project config; the synchronisation and its verification are shared code. Port the mechanism with the defect it caused recorded alongside it, so the next reader knows which case the code is defending against.
- `lib/cmd/docs` for `agents`, `treeindex`, `completions`, `index`, `publish`. D18 found the names agree 3/4 but each is a shell function rather than a command line, so these are implementations rather than catalogue rows.
- BATS coverage, with the sidecar case exercised against a project that has several.

## Dependencies

- WP-05 (`read_version`, `assert_semver`), WP-08 (catalogue).
- Blocks WP-10.

## Notes

Highest-risk family of the five. `version set` and `version bump` mutate files that other tooling reads, and a partial sync leaves a project internally inconsistent in a way no gate currently catches. Treat the sidecar write as all-or-nothing and prove it.
wps.preamble: Split out of WP-08 (built-in command library) along the family cut WP-08's own notes named.

wps.title: Built-ins: Shared, off by default
wps.objective: Ship the five commands that some projects want and most do not -- `which`, `macos`, `precommit`, `publish`, `content` -- disabled unless the config asks for them.
wps.body:
## Deliverables

- Each of the five implemented, and **off unless enabled**.
- **The opt-in activation axis itself.** D11 makes a built-in active exactly when its language is declared, which is the wrong test here: these five are language-agnostic and still should not appear uninvited. `macos` on a Linux project and `publish` on a private one are both noise at best. Today `_DEVBIN_BUILTIN_COMMANDS` lists all five, so they resolve in every project -- the gap is real and currently latent only because they exit 3.
- BATS coverage that an unenabled command is genuinely absent from the surface rather than present-and-failing.

## Dependencies

- WP-08 (catalogue and its activation rules).
- Blocks WP-10.

## Notes

The interesting content here is not the five commands, which are thin. It is the second activation axis: devbin now has language scoping (D11) and will need enablement scoping, and the two must compose without a project having to reason about their interaction.
wps.preamble: Split out of WP-08 (built-in command library) along the family cut WP-08's own notes named. Last of the five.

state.evidence: that file

criteria.text: The reader parses the documented subset: nested maps, scalar sequences, quoted scalars, inline and whole-line comments, blank lines, `---`, and dedent back to a parent path

Every construct outside the subset is refused with an error naming the file and the line: tabs, odd indent, jumped indent, duplicate keys, anchors/aliases, block scalars, flow collections, sequences of maps, malformed lines, illegal key characters

Accessors behave: `cfg_get` returns a default for an absent path and never prefix-matches; `cfg_has` distinguishes set from absent; `cfg_list` returns immediate children in document order, de-duplicated
Schema validation requires `project.name`, rejects unknown keys, and rejects keys nested deeper or shallower than the schema allows
The reader has no `yq` dependency: it never invokes yq, and it parses with yq absent from PATH
The reader runs on bash 3.2
Every schema key is documented with its default in a commented reference config

state.evidence: `lib/config.reference.yaml`

criteria.text: The dispatcher resolves its project root symlink-safely and works from any working directory, through a symlink, and under a project-named or short alias
Identity comes from config, not from the invoked filename, so `bin/<prj>` and `bin/<alias>` may both be symlinks to `bin/devbin`
Resolution follows D2's order: project handler, then config mapping, then built-in, then exit 2; a project handler shadows a built-in of the same name
Shadowing is total: a project handler displaces the built-in's option set, leaving only config-declared options
A built-in that is not yet implemented exits 3 with its reason, never a quiet success
`all` is synthesised from the active option list, runs every option in declared order, does not stop at the first breach, names every failure, and exits non-zero if any failed
An `in_all: false` option is excluded from `all` and REPORTED as skipped, and still runs when named directly

D11 activation holds: a built-in option is active when its language is declared, `enabled: false` deactivates at command or option level, and an explicitly declared option is active whatever the languages say
A command whose options are all inactive is itself inactive and absent from help
Deactivation is visible: asking for an inactive built-in explains why (language not declared, or disabled) rather than reporting an unknown option
Devbin runs its own gates through its own dispatcher, and `tests/gate` is deleted rather than kept alongside

state.evidence: `bin/devbin check all`, `bin/devbin test all`, `intent/llm/MODULES.md` watch-item resolved

criteria.text: Sub-dispatch is recursive per D3: one resolution rule applied at each level, so a third level (`db sql <stmt>`, `media covers`) routes by the same rule as the second

`all` is RESERVED wherever the command has declared options -- config-declared options compose with a project handler, so the sweep survives the shadow, and a sub-handler named `all` cannot thin it out; the one shape that receives `all` verbatim is a full project handler declaring NO options, whose argument list is wholly its own (refined during WP-10, whose corpus surface -- `which all`, `docs all` -- was unreachable under the unconditional reservation) -- and a bare `<command>` that HAS options prints that command's help rather than running everything -- and exits NON-ZERO, because naming no option is a usage error and a command that exits 0 having run nothing is a false green every `&&` chain misreads. Asking with `-h`/`--help` exits 0, since that request succeeded. A command with no options and a command line of its own -- a surface such as `server` -- runs it instead, since printing help would make the command unusable (clarified during WP-14, which found the original wording contradicted every launcher; the exit code corrected during WP-07, whose corpus audit found the ruling already written down in Laksa's authored help)
The exit-code contract holds across the surface: 0 ok, 1 die, 2 unknown command, 3 not built yet
`lib/helpers` loads and works with no other devbin library sourced, and reads no config -- a handler is a separate process that sources it alone
Double-sourcing any library is free (load guard), and the diagnostic prefix falls back to `devbin` before config is loaded

The output primitives behave as the corpus did: `die` exits 1 to stderr with the project prefix, `warn` continues, `not_yet` exits 3 naming what unblocks it, `require_tool` dies with the remedy, `init_colors` yields nothing when off or under `NO_COLOR`
`strip_ansi` removes CSI sequences and leaves plain text untouched
`abs_path` passes an absolute path through and absolutises a relative one against the project root

`read_version` resolves the corpus drift: it reads a bare `VERSION` file, extracts the version from `mix.exs`, `Cargo.toml` and `package.json`, honours the configured source, and answers `unknown` rather than failing when there is none
`assert_semver` accepts `X.Y.Z` and refuses anything else, quoting what it got
`rlwrap_exec` runs the command under rlwrap with history and any completions file, and degrades to a plain exec with a warning when rlwrap is absent

The corpus's four hand-written option setters collapse into one config-driven function: a valued option is validated against its declared set and exported, a value outside the set is refused naming what was expected, an option declaring no values accepts anything, and a flag exports `true` or the value config names
A shared option declaring no `export` target is a config error, not a silent no-op

`parse_common_opts` accepts both `--opt value` and `--opt=value`, leaves everything unrecognised in `DEVBIN_ARGS` with argument boundaries intact, consumes no following word for a flag, and refuses a valued option with nothing after it
The bash 3.2 empty-array trap is handled and proven: the guarded expansion yields zero words under `set -u` on the system bash, and the unguarded form is demonstrated to fail there
Shared options are parsed once by the dispatcher and reach the handler as environment; an undeclared option passes through to the handler; a bad value is refused before the handler runs
The whole stack -- config load, activation, `all` synthesis, shared options -- runs under `/bin/bash`, the bash 3.2 target
`is_command` answers from what actually resolves, so it cannot disagree with the dispatch surface
Every corpus divergence carries a ruling with its reason

state.evidence: `design.md` D13

criteria.text: The seal invariant holds: a green run's `.errors` is empty, a red run's is not, and the companion opens with an in-flight marker so a run aborted before sealing reads as not-green
Red is never empty even when nothing parses: a red run with no matching failure blocks, or whose log has vanished, still seals a header plus whatever tail could be recovered
The run log keeps its ANSI escapes and the sealed `.errors` is stripped, because the seal is the artifact a human quotes
Sealing is a no-op when no companion is kept, and a seal whose directory has vanished mid-run warns rather than failing silently
A promotion is appended to the log as well as printed, so a derived red verdict survives in the artifact and reaches the seal; a promotion that cannot be recorded warns
`LATEST_*` symlinks are created with relative targets and are a convenience only: every run prints its own absolute seal path, never the pointer
Purge deletes prior runs and keeps this run's pair, and NEVER deletes a file a `LATEST_*` pointer still resolves to -- including both members of the pair, since a dangling `.errors` reads green
`in_keepset` matches whole lines exactly and tolerates a leading dash; `purge-only` keeps the newest kept run by mtime rather than by name; `--purge` with `--no-out` is refused
Every named grammar extracts its tool's failure blocks and drops the structural and green lines: `mix`, `credo`, `cargo`, `xcodebuild`, `lua`, `shell`, `generic`
The xcodebuild grammar captures a swift-testing issue block and marks it when truncating, rather than silently dropping detail
An unknown grammar name falls back to `generic` with a warning rather than sealing with an empty extraction; documented aliases resolve to the same source

`run_gate` runs a command or a shell function, propagates its exit code, honours both option spellings, requires a suffix and a command, and rejects an unknown option rather than treating it as the command
`run_gate` does not change the caller's shell options: errexit is restored to whatever the caller had, on or off
Concurrent runs of one gate in one tree do not share or truncate a log: log creation is atomic, so each run gets its own pair and its own correct seal
The synthesised `all` points at the seal of every gate that failed, from a ledger the gates append to rather than from a `LATEST_*` pointer
Devbin's own gates run through `run_gate`, so a defect in the sealed-gate subsystem breaks Devbin's own build first

state.evidence: `bin/.devbin/cmd/check`, `bin/.devbin/cmd/test`

criteria.text: The global listing is GENERATED from what actually resolves: every active command appears with its summary and its active options, and no command list is hand-maintained anywhere (D4)

Commands are GROUPED, in the order `help.groups` declares. A group config does not name is appended in first-seen order, and a command with no group lands in a single trailing catch-all rather than vanishing from the listing

Summary, group and usage hint have ONE source each, read config first, then the resolving handler's own header, then the catalogue. What devbin ships is declared once in the catalogue; what a project ships is declared once in its handler; neither carries the other's copy (D23)
A handler dropped into `cmd/` is FIRST-CLASS in help with no config edit: its own group, its summary, its option list and its synthesised `all`, exactly as a built-in gets
`help <cmd>` prints authored long-form from `bin/.devbin/help/<cmd>.md` when it exists, and sub-topics resolve by the same rule at every depth (D3)
With no authored file `help <cmd>` still ANSWERS -- summary, usage, active options, where it resolves from -- rather than printing an empty page or an error
`help <unknown>` exits non-zero and says how to see what exists; an INACTIVE command is distinguished from an unknown one and says why it is not offered (D11)
The preamble and the shared-options block render from config, so the corpus's launcher-vs-product disambiguation and its `--env`/`--bin` block survive with no heredoc

`help --why` prints the listing plus, for each command, where it resolved from; and for every command and option devbin ships that is NOT offered here, the reason it is not. D2's order and D11's scoping become visible instead of presenting as absence
Drift is refused in BOTH directions, by a test rather than by review: every command the listing names resolves, and every command that resolves is named
Every authored topic across the four corpus launchers is inventoried with an explicit disposition; nothing authored is dropped silently

state.evidence: `intent/st/ST0001/help-migration.md`, 70 topics and 1,769 lines counted, five dispositions ruled, one embedded ruling extracted and fixed in the framework

criteria.text: Help is ONE subsystem in one file; the dispatcher parses and calls and holds no rendering (IN-AG-THIN-COORD-001)

state.evidence: `lib/help`, with AT-07.38 asserting `bin/devbin` names no renderer

criteria.text: The built-in catalogue is ONE table: `lib/resolve` keeps no copy of the command or option lists it held as placeholders
The catalogue answers language, grammar, log suffix, command line and summary for every option it carries, and returns non-zero for one it does not
A command line survives the table intact, including embedded `--` and multiple flags; a tier-1 option reports `@builtin` and still carries its other metadata
`build` ships NO option set (D18 tier 4), and `check parity` is absent -- both are name-only universality, and shipping either would impose one project's shape on the rest
Every catalogue option names a grammar devbin actually ships, and every `@builtin` option has a function implementing it
A built-in gate runs its catalogue command line through the sealed-gate runner with nothing declared in config, and seals green or red correctly with its declared grammar
Config's `run:` overrides a built-in option's command line, and a config-declared option is not swallowed by the built-in that owns its command
A built-in gate command refuses an unknown option by name and prints its usage when given none
Built-in commands are discoverable: `help` lists them with an otherwise-empty config, scoped to the declared languages, with summaries from the catalogue
A project handler still displaces the whole built-in option set, and is asked about its own options rather than having them vetted against the catalogue

One rig (D19): a config-declared option that declares `log:` seals through the same runner a built-in uses, with `log: true` naming the pair after the option, and `all` points at its seal exactly as it does a built-in's
An option that declares no `log:` runs bare, so a long-running interactive command is not teed
Gate logs resolve against the project root, so the verdict line names the file that was actually written, and a declared `run:` executes at the project root from any calling directory

The gate families run end to end against a real toolchain for every language Devbin itself declares: `check all` and `test all` execute the shipped shell gates through the dispatcher on both CI platforms, not via bats directly. The elixir, rust and swift gates have no toolchain in this repo and are exercised at WP-10 / WP-11

state.evidence: `.github/workflows/tests.yml` (`bin/devbin test all`, `bin/devbin check all` on ubuntu and macos), `bin/.devbin/config.yaml` declaring `shell` alone

criteria.text: `install` vendors the RUNNING runtime -- the dispatcher plus every file under `lib/` -- into the target's `bin/devbin` and `bin/.devbin/lib/`, so an already-installed devbin seeds another project by exactly the path a source checkout does

Install is idempotent and refuses to clobber: a second run over an existing install stops with the reason and names the flag that overrides it; with that flag the resulting tree is identical to a fresh install
Install NEVER writes over project content. A starter `config.yaml` appears only when there is none, and `--force` does not change that: it re-vendors the runtime and nothing else

The vendored/authored seam is ONE rule, stated once and asserted: everything under `bin/.devbin/lib/` is devbin's and is replaced wholesale; everything else under `bin/.devbin/` is the project's and is never touched
The symlinks D6 promises -- `bin/<project-name>` and `bin/<alias>` -> `devbin` -- are created, and a real file already sitting at either name is REFUSED rather than replaced
`manifest.sha256` records a checksum for every vendored file, plus the framework version and the source it came from, and is rewritten by upgrade
`upgrade` re-syncs from the recorded source (or `--from`) and REFUSES to overwrite a vendored file whose checksum no longer matches the manifest. An edit in place is reported, named, and left on disk
Upgrade reports a disposition for every file -- added, updated, unchanged, skipped -- and a run that changed nothing says so rather than printing an empty report
Upgrade with a missing, unreadable or non-devbin source fails naming the path it tried and the flag that overrides it, and writes NOTHING -- a half-replaced runtime is worse than a stale one

`doctor` reports per check: dispatcher present and executable, config parses and validates against the schema, `devbin_version` satisfied, manifest intact, every declared command resolves, no orphaned handler, symlinks intact, bash version noted

doctor exits non-zero when any check fails, and CANNOT report a clean bill having run nothing: the number of checks run is in its output, and a run that checks nothing is itself a failure (the AC-04.13 lesson, applied to a gate that predates it)
doctor catches the two failures that are otherwise silent -- a handler in `cmd/` that no command reaches, and a vendored file edited in place since install

`devbin_version` in config is a CONSTRAINT the project declares and doctor is what enforces it; a runtime outside the range is named as a mismatch carrying both versions, and the constraint is honoured on both sides of its bound

`new <cmd>` scaffolds a RUNNABLE command in one step -- an executable handler carrying its `# devbin:` header, a help stub and a test stub -- and the scaffolded command resolves and appears in help with no config edit. AC-07.4's promise, made operational
`new` refuses to overwrite an existing handler and refuses a name that is not a legal command name, naming which rule was broken

The catalogue carries option-less COMMAND rows in the one table: the row key is `<command>` with no option, `builtin_options_for` still reports no options for such a command, and no second table appears
A catalogue row is a gate or it is not: grammar and log suffix are both real or both absent, never one of each
Command-level resolution mirrors `run_option`'s order: project handler, then config's own `run:`, then the catalogue default, then declared-but-unrunnable
The D19 rule holds one level up: a command declaring `log:` seals through `run_gate`; one that does not runs bare
A launcher REPLACES the dispatcher process rather than running beneath it, so the terminal talks to the launched program directly

`cli` composes its command line from `project.name` rather than the catalogue gaining template substitution
`repl` runs through `rlwrap_exec`, and still works when `rlwrap` is absent
`server` runs the project's server, and its `--iex` variant when that flag is given
D20: a framework-owned option exports `DEVBIN_OPT_<NAME>` whether or not config declares it, and when a project declares its own `export:` the one parsed value reaches both names

criteria.text: D11 language scoping reaches COMMANDS, not only options: a built-in command whose catalogue row names a language is inactive where that language is not declared, and does not run the tool off the developer's PATH
An inactive command says WHY, as an inactive option already did: disabled-in-config and wrong-language are distinguishable from an unknown command

D11 language scoping reaches FRAMEWORK-OWNED OPTIONS too (issue 0001): a framework option is offered exactly where the commands that consume it are, so help cannot advertise `--iex` in a project that lists every surface as unavailable. Parsing and the listing scope through ONE predicate, so an option can be neither accepted-but-unadvertised nor advertised-but-unaccepted; a project wanting the flag regardless declares it in `options:` and config wins on shape

An output assertion cannot be silently disarmed by a bare `--`: the helpers read their pattern as the first argument, so the end-of-options marker becomes the pattern and the assertion tests nothing. Refused structurally, because a disarmed assertion still passes
`fmt` runs its catalogued options through the shared gate body, and `fmt all` is synthesised from the ACTIVE set so a project's declared languages decide what it formats

A missing formatter SKIPS loudly and does not fail the run -- `fmt` claims no verdict, so skipping is not a false green; the message is mandatory, because silence is indistinguishable from having formatted the files
`fmt md` formats root Markdown only unless given explicit paths, and says why: prettier strips the column alignment out of Markdown tables, and `intent/` and `docs/` are where the tables are
D21: `fmt --check` does not exist. The formatting gate is `check format`, it seals, and it does NOT skip when its tool is missing -- the asymmetry with AC-15.2 is what "a gate claims a verdict" means
`build` ships no default option set and is still fully functional from declared targets alone: they run, seal, appear in help, and `all` runs them in declared order (D18 tier 4's positive half)

The pairing holds by construction for EVERY arm, not one: each command line `check format` verifies is DERIVED from the `fmt` arm it verifies, and every `fmt` arm carrying a language has a check arm. A change to either without the other is caught. Broadened 2026-08-08 (issue 0003) -- the original wording named `fmt elixir` alone, which is exactly the gap it was meant to police: `fmt` had four arms and the gate verified one. `md` is deliberately excluded, and the exclusion is asserted rather than assumed, because a gate over Markdown would assert a verdict this project does not hold -- prettier re-pads tables and this repository hand-aligns them
`db` runs its catalogued core -- setup, migrate, reset, seed -- through the shared gate body, and any of them is overridden in one line of config

`db` REFUSES `MIX_ENV=prod`, names what it is protecting, and points at the project handler as the way past it rather than a flag. `db reset` drops the database, and only one of the four corpus projects guarded this
Sub-dispatch is recursive by one rule (D3, discharging AC-04.12): `<handler>.d/<sub>` resolves at the second level and `<handler>.d/<sub>.d/<leaf>` at the third, by the same test at each
A word that names no sub-handler is an ARGUMENT rather than an error, so a statement or migration name passes through to the handler untouched
The descent applies to devbin's own handlers as well as a project's -- one resolution rule, whoever supplied the handler

What `db` does NOT ship is recorded with its reason: `codegen` (an Ash task, not an Elixir one, so cataloguing it would offer it to Elixir projects that have no Ash) and `proxy` (Laksa's and Lamplight's are the same algorithm, but it encodes a hosting provider)

criteria.text: `version` reads: bare prints `<name> <version>`, `show` prints the bare number for scripting, and both read the file `project.version_from` names
`set` and `bump` share one semver implementation: `set` refuses a non-semver without writing, `bump` advances the named part and zeroes those to its right, and an unknown part is refused

Sidecars fan out BY FILE KIND. Config names the files; the library holds the recipe for each (D1), so a project's config carries no regular expressions. A rewrite touches the version and nothing next to it

Derived files are written FIRST and the version file LAST, so a partial failure leaves the version un-advanced and a rerun recomputes the same target rather than double-bumping. A missing sidecar is named, never silently skipped

`sync` is UNCONDITIONAL: it heals a lagging sidecar even when the version file already holds the target, which is the exact case a "only if it differs" gate skips and the one that shipped a wrong CFBundleShortVersionString
`check` reports drift, names the file and what it found, writes nothing, exits non-zero, and points at the command that heals it

There is ONE reader. `check` reads sidecars through `read_version` rather than its own extractors -- a reader and a writer that disagree about which line they mean is how `check` comes to pass a file `set` would rewrite differently

`docs` ships `agents` and `treeindex` and only those. `treeindex` REFUSES the project root and an absolute path, names a directory it cannot find rather than passing, and does not abandon the rest when one entry is bad
What `docs` does NOT ship is recorded with its reason: `completions` (two of four), `index` and `publish` (one each) encode where a project keeps its output

state.evidence: `lib/cmd/docs` header

criteria.text: An opt-in built-in is ABSENT from a project that has not asked for it -- not present-and-failing, which is what all five were before this WP
Asking for one says it is shipped but not enabled, and names the config key that enables it. D11's visibility rule, applied to the new axis
`enabled: true` switches one on and it appears in help with the catalogue's summary; `enabled: false` still wins over everything

The two axes compose without a project reasoning about them: language scoping still governs language-scoped built-ins, enablement governs opt-in ones, and a project handler activates either by its presence alone (D2)
devbin ships NO command line for any of the five (D18 tier 4, five times over): each is one or two of the four projects and encodes that project's shape

# WP-10 equivalence evidence -- Conflab, old launcher vs devbin

Collected 2026-08-09, with both launchers present and canonical (`bin/conflab` = the old launcher, untouched since `565cddad`; `bin/devbin` = the vendored runtime at Devbin `e0ed389`). Conflab tree at `5244683d`. Old-side and new-side toolchain runs were SEQUENCED, never concurrent -- they share `_build/` and both `target/` dirs. Covers AC-10.8 (transcripts), AC-10.9 (what each gate EXAMINED), AC-10.11 (seals + verdict lines), AC-10.12 (real-toolchain runs incl `test all --purge`), AC-10.13 (shims untouched).

## The examines table (AC-10.9)

Counts are quoted from the named seal logs, which are the record; this file is the comparison of them.

| Gate            | Old side (seal)                                    | New side (seal)                                    | Verdict          |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| test mix        | 2323 passed, 12 excluded (`20260809-1338.mix`)     | 2323 passed, 12 excluded (`20260809-1337.MIX`)     | IDENTICAL        |
| test rust (cli) | 329 passed (`20260809-1339.rust`)                  | 329 passed (`20260809-1336.RUST`)                  | IDENTICAL        |
| test rust (dmn) | 1189 passed (same log, second trailer)             | 1189 passed (same log, second trailer)             | IDENTICAL        |
| test swift      | 373 tests, 49 suites (`20260809-1339.swift`)       | 373 tests, 49 suites (`20260809-1336.SWIFT`)       | IDENTICAL        |
| test credo      | 3904 mods/funs, no issues (`20260809-1339.credo`)  | 3904 mods/funs, no issues (`20260809-1337.CREDO`)  | IDENTICAL        |
| check format    | exit 0                                             | exit 0, empty `FORMAT` seal                        | MATCH (green)    |
| check clippy    | exit 0                                             | exit 0, empty `CLIPPY` seal                        | MATCH (green)    |
| check contract  | 2 checks, 6 spellings (2a probe)                   | identical output, sealed                           | IDENTICAL        |
| check parity    | 63/56 surface counts (2a probe)                    | identical output, sealed                           | IDENTICAL        |
| check deps      | exit 1, names 9 unused deps                        | exit 1, names the SAME 9, sealed                   | IDENTICAL (red)  |
| check toolchain | exit 1, elixir 1.20.2->1.20.3, erlang 29.0.4->.5   | exit 1, the SAME two skews, sealed                 | IDENTICAL (red)  |

The two red gates are the strongest rows in the table: both launchers, run on the same tree minutes apart, report the same breaches with the same facts and nothing else. The reds are real project/machine state (unused deps in mix.lock; a toolchain upgraded past its pin), not migration artifacts, and they are hv's to clean or accept -- not this migration's to touch.

The `:known_broken` exclusion (12 tests) is active on both sides -- the ruling in the old test help survived the port.

## Deliberate examines DIFFERENCES, on the record

- **version check**: old examines 6 sidecar entries including the three Cargo.lock package lines; new examines VERSION + the three declared sidecars, with the locks owned by the release handler (hv ruling 1, delta 1). Both exit 0 on the synced tree. The new side checks LESS by design and the difference has a named owner -- this is the AC-10.1 correction carried visibly, not a silent narrowing.
- **check format** covers Elixir + both Rust crates on both sides (the config-declared gate restored the old coverage; the catalogue's elixir-only row does not serve here).

## Seals and verdict lines (AC-10.11)

Every new-side gate printed `verdict: <abs path>` and left a `.errors` companion that is empty exactly when that run was green: the four test seals and FORMAT/CLIPPY/CONTRACT/PARITY/COMPILE/CRITIC are 0 bytes; DEPS and TOOLCHAIN are non-empty and name their breaches. The run's terminal exit agreed with the seals in this pass, but the seals are the record.

## The full-fat purge (AC-10.12)

`bin/devbin test all --purge` ran the real toolchain end to end and fanned `--purge` to all four gates. Each purged 0 files -- correct: purge is scoped to its own gate's suffix family, and the only prior uppercase-suffix runs were the current pairs. The old launcher's lowercase-suffix seals (`.mix.`, `.swift.`, ...) are invisible to devbin's purge by construction, so the old evidence survives the migration period. **Step-4 checklist consequence: after the switch, the lowercase seal files in tmp/test and tmp/check are permanent orphans -- one hand-clean, once, in or beside the delete-only commit.**

## Transcripts (AC-10.8)

Byte-identical old-vs-new: bare `use` (the full flavour report), `which all` (the full resolution walk, stamps included). Same-behaviour with adapted text: every usage path (-h exits 0; bare exits 1 on build/daemon/app/docs/macos/release per the corpus's own bare-command ruling; unknown subs refused naming the real surface). `db all` is now the db handler's own refusal listing setup|migrate|codegen|reset|seed|sql|proxy, where the interim dispatcher answer was "has no options to run" -- fixed at Devbin `e0ed389`. Authored help renders through the new path with the project's markdown convention (delta 10): content and rulings preserved, typography deliberately not byte-identical.

## Shims (AC-10.13)

server, deploy, macos, release, repl, flysql, precommit-rust: all last touched `565cddad` (2026-08-05, pre-migration), none modified in the working tree. Every migration commit left them alone.

## Coverage statement -- what this pass did NOT compare

- `check compile` old-side was not re-run in this pass (`--warnings-as-errors --force` rebuilds everything); the new side's COMPILE seal is empty. The old side's routine green through this week is assumption, not measurement here.
- deploy, release, macos and precommit were probed at the usage surface only -- they are owner-authorised actions and were not executed live. Their equivalence rests on the ported source reading plus the delegation structure (they call the same `check`/`test` gates measured above).
- `fmt` (mutating) and `docs` (writes derived files) were not executed live; surface and refusal paths probed only.
- `bin/cf` still points at the old launcher; the alias switch is step 4's.

# Conflab surface inventory

Read-only survey of Conflab's launcher ahead of WP-10, taken 2026-08-08 against Conflab as it stands (25 files, 4,610 lines under `bin/`). Nothing in Conflab was written to. This is the evidence the WP-10 config is DERIVED from rather than invented, and it is the "before" half of the equivalence evidence WP-10 owes -- you cannot prove every command still works without first writing down what worked.

Method: every handler read, the helper library read end to end, and each mapping claim checked against devbin's actual catalogue and schema rather than against the design narrative. Where a claim is a finding, it was reproduced by running it.

## The command surface -- 18 commands

`CONFLAB_COMMANDS` (`bin/conflab_helpers:127`) is the single source: `server iex cli daemon app use which build test check fmt db docs version macos release deploy precommit`. Eighteen exactly, which is what WP-10's brief says.

| `iex`       | built-in as-is                     | catalogue default `iex -S mix` matches; Conflab adds the same `.env` sourcing          |
| `cli`       | built-in + project handler         | needs `resolve_native_bin`, so the handler stays project-local                         |

| `fmt`       | built-in, 4 options                | `elixir` `rust` `swift` `md` all present                                               |

**Nine project handlers, not the brief's six.** The six it names are right -- `app` `daemon` `use` `release` `macos` `deploy` -- and `which` and `precommit` are not a seventh and eighth, because they are `opt-in` catalogue rows WP-18 shipped deliberately without command lines, so Conflab declares the recipe and the row supplies the identity.

Three more need handlers the brief does not list, and none of them is a project-specific COMMAND -- each is a built-in whose surrounding behaviour is project-specific:

- `cli` -- needs `resolve_native_bin`, so which of three installed binaries runs is decided project-side.
- `server` and `iex` -- both source `config/.env` before exec. `lib/cmd/server`'s own header already rules this out of the framework by name ("Laksa prints a banner of URLs, Conflab sources config/.env ... none of that belongs to a framework") and gives the two ways out: a config `run:` or a project handler. A `run:` cannot do it -- sourcing a file then exec'ing is a script, and putting one in config is what D1 forbids -- so it is a handler.

That last pair matters more than it looks. Conflab's `server` warns when `config/.env` is absent, precisely because a missing provider key "looks identical to a revoked one three screens later". A migration that drops the sourcing does not fail; it boots on defaults and fails somewhere else.

`test` -- four gates, `mix` `credo` `rust` `swift`, all four already in the catalogue with matching command lines and grammars. This is the cleanest part of the migration and it is not a coincidence: `lib/runlog` is a port of Conflab's own sealed-gate subsystem (WP-06).

**The Swift grammar was checked specifically, because it is the one with a history.** Conflab's carries a late repair -- the swift-testing rules were missing and their absence INVERTED the seal, sealing 18 bytes for an assertion failure and 4.5 KB of log tail for a codesign failure. A port taken before that repair would reintroduce it. Devbin's has all four failure shapes, the `recorded an issue` block and the 40-line truncation marker, and it goes further than Conflab's: the three status glyphs are spliced in as bytes rather than written as literals, because `\xNN` is a gawk extension and a silently non-matching rule "would look like success, on the one grammar whose history is precisely that of an inverted seal". Faithful, hardened, and ASCII-clean. No finding.
